Q1 2025 E-Commerce VC Trends
VC activity
Deal and exit activity
Deal activity rebounds in Q1, but a longer-term plateau persists
In Q1 2025, e-commerce enablement VC deal activity outperformed Q4 2024 levels in both deal 
count (up 14.5%) and value (up 7.1%). The 134 transactions closed marked the highest deal count 
since Q1 2023, and the $2.9 billion invested was the highest deal value since Q4 2023 ($3.2 billion). 
The past nine quarters represent a new steady state in e-commerce, averaging $2.4 billion 
across 119 rounds, albeit with pressure to the downside. Looking at the broader trend, the 2014 
to 2019 period marked a steady upward trajectory for e-commerce investment; a crescendo 
during the COVID-19 pandemic pulled forward digital commerce demand; and now, the 2023 to 
2025 window reflects a plateau and a modest retreat in investor enthusiasm. For the remainder 
of 2025, we expect deal activity to remain flat until greater clarity is reached regarding the 
macroeconomic landscape.
Tariffs introduce near-term spending friction
In the near term, the impact of tariffs on B2B software-as-a-service (SaaS) spending may remain 
unsettled. Wide-ranging tariffs can increase prices, adversely impact shopper purchasing 
decisions, and erode merchant margins. Downstream, this could affect technology investment 
decisions as brands face tightening capital constraints. 
Merchants will form two camps: those that embrace austerity, pause all in-flight purchasing 
decisions, and seek to rein in costs; and those that lean into operational efficiency and enablement

via software and AI to generate a demand pull-forward. Assuming broad-spectrum tariffs 
are implemented as part of a protectionist economic agenda from the Trump administration, 
we anticipate a contraction in SaaS spending that will weigh down VC-backed e-commerce 
enablement vendors. 
Agentic AI and interactive commerce begin to collide
In the long term, the steady embrace of digital commerce will be unabated as the role and 
utility of brick-and-mortar retail evolve in real time. Through Q1, e-commerce’s share of all retail 
transactions stands at 16.2%,1 alongside a net-contraction in store closures through year-end 
2024.2 Looking further ahead, early signals point to a potential platform shift in digital commerce—
one where agentic AI and interactive entertainment converge to redefine how consumers 
discover, engage with, and purchase products. Early movers are already laying the groundwork 
for this transformation through immersive integrations and AI-driven interfaces. Perplexity is 
integrating product results into its answer engine, Shopify is formalizing an integration with 
Roblox, and Anthropic is pioneering a model context protocol that will pave the way for agent-to-
agent interactions. Presently, incumbents and early-movers are best positioned to capitalize on 
these shifts as many startups face similar business model, incentive, and lock-in constraints from 
previous technology waves.
Of course, the demands of the immediate future siphon finite merchant resources. The staccato shock 
of tariffs on supply chains demands that merchants shift their focus to looming Black Friday orders, 
empty shelves during the holidays, and technology simplification rather than agentic commerce. 
Early-stage investment regains momentum
Early-stage activity continued a recovery that started in H1 2023 when deal activity concentrated 
in late-stage and venture-growth rounds. At the time, later-stage rounds outnumbered earlier-
stage rounds in a nearly 60/40 split, reflecting a flight to perceived safety. Established startups 
with proven revenue models, customer traction, and operational maturity were seen as lower risk 
amid macro uncertainty. Early-stage teams, by contrast, faced higher scrutiny as limited track 
records made it harder to justify investment in an environment where durability and near-term 
viability were at a premium. But in Q2 2024, the pendulum began to swing back toward early-stage 
activity, resulting in a 56/44 split by the start of 2025. 
Valuations rise, but uncertainty looms in H2 2025
The median pre-money valuation for the e-commerce sector jumped from $46.8 million in full-
year 2024 to $83.1 million in Q1 2025, propped up by outlier valuations at the venture-growth 
stage. However, divergent trajectories underpin this top-line trend. The median pre-seed/seed 
pre-money valuation increased modestly from full-year 2024 to Q1 2025 but has remained 
between $10 million and $15 million since 2021. 
Looking forward, the loose connection between public market fluctuations and venture valuations 
will take time to strengthen. Markets had rebounded by the start of Q2, and if that momentum 
holds—buoyed by tariff relief and a soft-landing narrative—high valuations could persist through 
1: “E-Commerce Retail Sales as a Percent of Total Sales,” Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, U.S. Census Bureau, May 19, 2025.
2: “Store Closures Outpace Openings Amid ‘Historic Shift’ to Service-Based Tenants,” Retail Dive, Nate Delesline III, February 21, 2025.

the second half of the year. However, if inflation reaccelerates and the Federal Reserve is forced to 
tighten its policies, or if economic conditions deteriorate into a recession, startup valuations could 
face sharp downward resets, especially valuations for capital-intensive businesses.3 Early-stage 
valuations began trending upward in 2022, while late-stage valuations fell in Q1 2025.
The median pre-money valuation step-up for the e-commerce sector increased from 1.5x in full-
year 2024 to 1.8x in Q1 2025, representing a continued recovery since 2023. Excluding seed deals, 
which fell from 1.4x to 1.1x in the same period, all other stages increased, led by venture growth 
(increasing from 1.2x to 1.8x), followed by the early stage (increasing from 1.7x to 2.4x).
Leading segments emerge across the enablement landscape
On a deal value basis, the purchase medium segment outpaced all other segments with $1.1 billion 
invested across 22 deals in Q1, while horizontal platforms led on a volume basis with 44 deals 
totaling $903.6 million. The quarter’s leading subsegments include e-commerce as a service with 
$463.6 million across 13 deals, livestream & social commerce with $270.5 million across four 
deals, and storefronts & headless APIs with $260.3 million across 14 deals. Subsegments touching 
adjacent verticals, such as payment (touching fintech) and fulfillment & delivery (touching supply 
chain tech), were also active, raising $815.3 million and $195 million, respectively. 
Several notable deals in the quarter underscore these subsegment trends. The 2024 holiday 
season demonstrated the viability of livestream commerce as Whatnot raised a $265 million 
Series E. Vertical-specific platforms remain viable—as seen with AgVend’s $42.8 million deal 
and Goose’s $13.4 million deal—and several personalization platforms raised sizable rounds, 
including Hightouch ($80 million), prettydamnquick ($25 million), AMP ($20 million), and Instant 
($18 million). Resale platform Archive raised a $30 million Series B, reflecting how re-commerce 
stands to benefit from potential tariff-driven price increases. Inventory management continued to 
modernize with rounds for Swap ($40 million), Stockly ($26.9 million), and Pipe17 ($19.4 million). 
Exit activity sluggish despite pockets of M&A strength
VC and PE exit activity in the e-commerce sector was subdued at the start of the year, with 23 
deals totaling $868.6 million, pacing below an underwhelming 2024. At the current run rate, exit 
activity across both VC and PE would contract by 9.2% and 60.6%, respectively. The current pace 
would yield the lowest annual exit value since 2014 ($1.8 billion) and 2016 ($783.9 million). Across 
the broader US venture ecosystem, top-line exit value improved in Q1 but was top-heavy, propped 
up by CoreWeave’s IPO and Google’s acquisition of Wiz. 
While several consumer-facing startups have either listed or announced plans to list publicly, 
including Klarna, StubHub, and Discord, many processes were halted as uncertainty roiled 
markets following on-again-off-again tariff machinations. However, equity markets are ripping 
after the Trump administration announced progress in negotiations for tariff reductions. Yet, if US

consumers slow their spending, public market headwinds and lower risk appetites could materially 
weigh on B2C businesses and dampen interest in consumer and commerce-enablement platforms. 
In Q1, M&A activity was slightly better across closed deals. The quarter’s 32 deals produced 
$3.8 billion, pacing fairly compared with 2024’s 90 deals totaling $5.4 billion. Notable exits in the 
quarter included personalization platform Rokt’s acquisition of mParticle for $300 million, SPS 
Commerce’s acquisition of Carbon6 for $210 million, PSG’s LBO of streaming commerce platform 
Uscreen for $150 million, and Aquiline Capital Partners’ $110 million LBO of direct-to-consumer 
wine platform WineDirect. 
Emerging trends
Consumers navigate a turbulent Q1
Signaling potential weakness in consumer demand, US retail sales undulated in Q1, sputtering in 
January but jumping in March in anticipation of future price increases. Tariff threats erased 2025 
stock market gains and pulled down US GDP growth estimates for Q1 to 0.3% (from 2.3% in Q4) 
while eliciting outcries from the business community.4 The US economy’s underlying bifurcation 
remains pronounced: Top-decile earners account for nearly half of domestic spending.5 Across 
all other income brackets, consumption outlays declined—even as households tapped into their 
remaining excess savings—signaling that pandemic-era buffers are no longer sufficient to sustain 
spending in the face of rising costs.6 
With the Q4 holiday season in the rearview mirror, US consumers continued to rely on credit to 
finance everyday purchases, pushing household debt up 0.5% QoQ alongside modest increases in 
delinquencies.7 The US economy remained near full employment in Q1, despite a rash of headline-
grabbing layoffs across the federal workforce, as the unemployment rate hovered at 4%.8
Enablement vendors brace for impact
Exogenous shocks, such as tariff threats, cloud the outlook for e-commerce enablement vendors 
that are downstream of merchants attempting to protect already thin profit margins. Some 
retailers have paused or killed in-flight SaaS sales processes or hiring until a better sight line is 
established. Others are investing with ruthless prioritization of mission-critical key performance 
indicators, leveraging technology to drive operational efficiency. A recent memo from Shopify 
CEO Tobias Lütke emphasizing “reflexive AI usage” could prove prescient,9 signaling the end of 
optional AI use. 
In the near term, we expect merchants to solve for faster implementation timelines, higher return 
on investment, and lower technology overhead. Inventory management, price optimization,

order orchestration, and personalization/loyalty platforms are positioned relatively well, while 
vendors primarily targeting small and medium-size businesses face challenges because they 
lack the bargaining power to rapidly shift supply chains and benefited from soon-to-expire de 
minimis exemptions. 
Agentic AI inches toward impact
We pointed to an agentic AI future in our 2024 Consumer Technology Outlook. Agentic AI 
broadly refers to bots that can “think” ahead to anticipate business or shopper needs and make 
corresponding decisions, such as predicting a weather pattern and stocking inventory, thereby 
exhibiting a degree of agency. This modality is not new, as consumers have bemoaned automated 
bot behavior for years following anticipated shoe or concert-ticket drops. But the past six months 
have demonstrated an acceleration on all fronts. OpenAI introduced Operator, and Anthropic 
announced that Claude 3.7 Sonnet can act autonomously, albeit rudimentarily. In e-commerce, 
both incumbents and startups are developing their own agentic AI offerings. Amazon launched 
“Buy for Me,” Qeen.ai supports internal operations, and Intercom’s Fin targets postpurchase 
support with resolution-based pricing. Industry awareness of agentic AI took another step forward 
at the 2025 National Retail Federation conference. Salesforce’s presence was robust to support the 
launch of its AI agent, Agentforce, and NVIDIA’s footprint was its most significant in years.
E-commerce is in a transition phase. The sector has certainly progressed from Salesforce’s Einstein 
and early iterations of algorithmic pricing, but merchants are still in the early innings of thinking 
through the implications of agent-to-agent experiences amid an era defined by unpredictable 
shocks—such as tariff swings, supply chain disruptions, and abrupt shifts in consumer demand—
that challenge long-term technology planning. For example, online traffic to US retail websites 
from generative AI referrals increased 1,200% between July 2024 and February 2025.10
Legacy systems strain under modern fulfillment demands
Order orchestration and inventory management are increasingly complicated and precise 
practices for merchants. The number of purchase venues is increasing, supply chains and 
input sourcing are perilous, and fulfillment options are diversifying amid unforgiving shopper 
expectations. The need for process orchestration—technology that coordinates disparate systems 
using business rules across front- and back-end systems—is emerging. Despite digital commerce’s 
growing share of retail transactions, few enterprise resource planning platforms were designed 
to accommodate current market demands or technical complexity in an era where purchase 
decisions are made at the speed of internet virality. 
The consequences of inaccuracy are material: Lost sales, delayed or canceled orders, and stale 
inventory estimates can push shoppers into the open arms of behemoths such as Amazon or 
Walmart. Order orchestration services fill an increasingly critical role in providing real-time 
inventory insights, creating streamlined views of product availability, responding rapidly to supply/
demand shifts, and more.11 Some example platforms include viax, Emporix, and Occtoo, as well as 
a variety of order management systems such as Kibo Commerce and Fluent Commerce that offer 
native functionality in these services. 
10: “Adobe Analytics: Traffic to U.S. Retail Websites From Generative AI Sources Jumps 1,200 Percent,” Adobe, Vivek Pandya, March 17, 2025.
11: “The Order Orchestration Imperative,” Cocktails & Commerce, Brian Walker and Bill Friend, January 2025.
